analytic.title: Real-Time Scheduling and Analysis of Processing Chains on Multi-threaded Executor in ROS 2

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: ROS (Robot Operating System) is currently one of the most popular development frameworks for robotic software, which is usually subject to hard real-time constraints in safecritical domains. Designers must formally model and analyze its timing behaviors to guarantee that real-time constraints are always honored at run-time. This paper studies real-time scheduling and analysis under a multi-threaded executor in ROS 2. We present a formal description of the scheduling model of multi-threaded executors, and develop response time analysis techniques for processing chains executing on it. Moreover, we identify a risk of increasing the response time of chains that may be caused by improper design when deploying systems on multi-threaded executors, which provides a useful guidance to designers. We conduct experiments with both randomly generated workloads and case studies on a realistic ROS 2 platform to evaluate and demonstrate our results. 27 2022 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The Robot Operating System (ROS) [1] is one of the most popular open-source software frameworks for robotics applications [2], [3], and is undergoing rapid development [4]. A main philosophy of ROS is to promote productivity of robotic software development by facilitating software modularity and composability. However, ROS also suffers a major shortcoming of lacking real-time capability, which limits its implementation in safety-critical environment [5]. For this context, ROS 2 [6], the second-generation ROS is released since 2017, which inherits the most positive aspects from ROS and aims to provide strong real-time capability to support real-time robotic software. For example, ROS 2 adopts DDS (Data Distribution Service) [7] as inter-process communication middleware for real-time data exchange, and can be deployed on top of real-time operating systems. The new architecture of ROS 2 provides a good foundation, but on its own is insufficient to support hard real-time robotic software.

Robotic software in safe-critical domains is usually subject to hard real-time constraints, so designers must formally model and analyze its timing behaviors to guarantee that real-time constraints are always honored at run-time. A core component relevant to the real-time performance of ROS 2 is the executor, which coordinates the execution of workload in the threads of underlying Operating System (OS). ROS 2 has two built-in executors: a single-threaded executor that executes workload in sequential and a multi-threaded executor that distributes Corresponding author: Dong Ji, email: jidong@cse.neu.edu.cn the execution of workload across multiple threads. Recently, several work [8]- [14] has studied modeling and analyzing real-time performance of ROS 2 single-threaded executor. It turns out that the scheduling behavior of ROS 2 executor is quite different from those studied in past real-time scheduling research and requires new analysis techniques. Although these studies have made it possible to guarantee the real-time performance of systems deployed on ROS 2 single-threaded executors, the problem of modeling and analysis of ROS 2 multi-threaded executor is still open.

As modern robotic applications are getting increasingly more complex, it is often necessary to implement them on multi-threaded executors to fully explore the computing capacity of multi-core processors. In this paper, we conduct the first work on real-time performance analysis of ROS 2 multi-threaded executors. We present the scheduling model of systems implemented as processing chains that are deployed on a multi-threaded executor, and develop response time analysis techniques for them. Moreover, we study the impact of the scheduling behaviors to the response time under different executors, and identify a risk of increasing response time when merging workload from multiple single-threaded executors into one multi-threaded executor in the design. We conduct experiments with both randomly generated workload and case studies on a realistic ROS 2 platform to evaluate and demonstrate our results.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND A. ROS 2
div.p: We first briefly introduce some background about ROS 2 and the context of our system model (a more detailed introduction to ROS 2 can be found in [8], [10], [11], [14], [15]). ROS 2 is a unified implementation of multiple abstraction layers above the Operating System (OS) (as shown in Fig. 1-(a)). ROS 2 applications are typically composed of individual nodes which communicate with each other using the publishsubscribe paradigm: nodes publish messages on topics, which broadcast the messages to nodes subscribed to the topic. Nodes react to incoming messages by activating callbacks to process each message. Since callbacks may publish messages themselves, complex behavior can be implemented as a network of topics and callbacks. To deploy a ROS 2 application, the individual nodes are distributed to hosts and then mapped to processes in the underlying OS. The executors in the ROS 2 client library coordinate the execution of callbacks of the nodes in the OS processes. ROS 2 provides two built-in executors: a single-threaded executor that executes callbacks in one thread, and a multi-threaded executor that distributes the processing of callbacks across multiple threads. Message exchanging between the publishers and the subscribers of nodes is realized by an abstract Data Distribution Service (DDS) layer, which is the communication interface between DDS and the client library, where DDS is an industry standard distributed communication system to exchange messages between the publishers and the subscribers. The timing behavior of single-threaded executor has been substantially studied in [8], [10], [16]. In this paper, we focus on applications that are implemented as processing chains (as shown in Fig. 1-(b)) executing on a multi-threaded executor. Each vertex in the chain represents a callback. A processing chain is triggered by some specific event (typically time event activated by a system timer) and spans over multiple executors. We limit our attention to computing the response time bound for a chain on a single executor. Nevertheless, our result can be extended to the case where a chain spans over multiple executors by adding the response time bound derived for each executor to calculate the end-to-end response time of the entire chain, referring to techniques such as Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA) approach [17]- [19].

Callbacks in an executor may belong to different callbackgroups. There are two types of callback group: mutually exclusive and reentrant. At run-time, the rules for scheduling callbacks in different types of callback groups are different (this will be explained later in Section. III-B). Callbacks may also belong to different nodes. In ROS 2, callbacks in the same node that are not specified to any callback group are considered in the same mutually exclusive callback group by default. Except for this, the notion of node is irrelevant from the analysis problem studied in this paper. Therefore, for simplicity, we will not include the node-level information in our abstract model.

div.head: B. Scheduling of multi-threaded executor
div.p: In the following, we introduce the scheduling behavior under a multi-threaded executor in ROS 2, which is based on a careful inspection of the source codes and related documentations 1 . To validate the model, we conduct substantial 1 Contents in this paper are based on ROS 2 Foxy Fitzroy [4].

experiments that include various configurations, and trace the resulting behavior with a tracing tool ROS2 tracing [11] to characterize each factor that may interfere the execution. Callback is the minimal scheduling entity in ROS 2 for the designer to handle. In a multi-threaded executor, threads take messages from the abstract DDS layer and execute the corresponding callbacks.

All threads in an executor maintain a common set wait set to record callbacks with available messages. A thread must hold a mutually exclusive lock low priority wait mutex before it accesses wait set. That is, wait set can only be accessed and modified by at most one thread at any time. Otherwise, the thread is blocked, waiting for the lock to be released.

When holding the lock, the thread looks for a callback to execute by searching through different categories of callbacks in a fixed order, which effectively attributes callbacks with different priorities. As introduced in [8], [10], [16], in ROS 2, the priority of a callback (i.e., the position in the order to be selected) is decided on two levels: (1) callback type: callbacks are classified into four types: timer, subscriber, service and client. Overall, the priority order of the four callback types is timer subscriber service client, where means "has higher priority than". (2) registration order: the priorities of callbacks of the same type depend on their registration order, and the one which registers earlier has a higher priority. It was introduced in some previous literature [8], [10] that timer callbacks follow different scheduling rules from other callbacks, which is no longer the case since ROS 2 Eloquent Elusor [12]. For simplicity, we will not include the information about the callback types in the rest of the paper.

A callback in wait set (with available messages) from a reentrant callback group can be selected. In contrast, each mutually exclusive callback group has a flag can be taken from to identify whether a callback belonging to it can be selected for execution. When a callback in this group is selected for execution, the flag is set to be false, and then set to be true after the callback finishes. A callback belonging to a mutually exclusive callback group can only be selected when the corresponding flag can be taken from is true. Otherwise the thread skips this callback and moves on to the next. Once a callback is successfully selected, the thread releases low priority wait mutex and removes the callback from wait set. If the configuration of yield before execute is set to be false, the thread starts to execute the selected callback immediately. Otherwise, if yield before execute is set to be true, the thread will yield the processor to the OS until it is scheduled again. In this work, we consider the default configuration yield before execute=false. In particular, the callback is executed with its earliest arrived message non-preemptively. 2If all categories have been checked and no callback can be selected for execution, the thread enters into wait for work (still holding the lock), resets wait set, waits for new messages, and then updates wait set. Similar with the scheduling process, a callback with available messages from a mutually exclusive callback group can only be added into wait set when the corresponding flag can be taken from is true.

When no callbacks can be added into wait set, to avoid the overhead caused by frequent locking and unlocking, the thread is blocked until it is notified by the arriving of new messages or reaches time out with respect to a predefined maximum blocking time. More specifically, the waiting process is realized by a function wait for in C++ standard library. Whether the thread will spin on the processor or suspend depends on the OS implementation. 3 Nevertheless, since wait set can only be updated when no callback can be selected for execution, this may not cause a utilization loss for the multi-threaded executor itself.
If still failing to find any callback to execute, the thread releases the lock and becomes idle. Fig. 2 illustrates the workflow of a thread to schedule callbacks.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In the following, we introduce a scheduling model covering the real-time related behaviors of a multi-threaded executor that we extract from the above description. For simplicity, we assume the overhead caused by threads accessing or updating wait set is zero. Notations used in this paper are summarized in TABLE I.

div.p: i is released, whereas another callback instance in J k i is released at the finishing time of its predecessor, i.e., at the time point when its input message from its predecessor is available. When multiple instances of the same callback are released, they are enqueued into a FIFO with regard to their release times. A callback instance c i,j is said to be pending when it is released and all its previous instances are either executing or finished. A pending callback instance c i,j can either be ready or P-blocked:

• If c i,j belongs to a mutually exclusive callback group, then c i,j is ready when no instances of callbacks in the same callback group as c i,j (including c i,j itself) are executing. Otherwise, c i,j is P-blocked. • If c i,j belongs to a reentrant callback group, then c i,j is always ready when it is pending. The executor maintains a ready set Ω, which records ready callback instances that can be selected for execution. Being eligible is the prerequisite for a ready callback instance c i,j in Ω to be selected, which also depends on the type of the callback group that c i,j belongs to. A callback instance c i,j in Ω which belongs to a mutually exclusive callback group is eligible when no instances of callbacks in the same callback group as c i,j are executing, otherwise it is R-blocked. In contrast, a callback instance belonging to a reentrant callback group is always eligible when it is in Ω. In other words, at any time, a callback instance in Ω is either eligible or Rblocked. From the above description, we can see that callback instances of callbacks in the same mutually exclusive callback group may never execute in parallel.

A callback instance is not added into Ω immediately when it is ready. Instead, a ready callback instance can only be added into Ω when there are no eligible callbacks in Ω and a thread is idle. We say Ω is updated at a time point when new elements are added into Ω. Moreover, when Ω is updated, Ω is firstly set to be ∅, and then all currently ready callback instances are added into Ω. In particular, we define time points when Ω is updated as polling points. We say a set of callback instances are in the same batch if they are added into Ω at the same polling point.
Eligible callback instances in Ω are selected one-by-one by m threads to execute non-preemptively. Recall that each (a)

div.head: IV. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: Unless explicitly specified, in the following, we will drop the indices and use C to present the analyzed chain. We focus on the analysis of an arbitrary chain instance of C, which is denoted by J. J is released at time r and finishes at time f . Accordingly, we use c i to represent the i th callback instance in J, which is released at r i and starts to execute at s i , where i ∈ [1, |C|]. All the other chains rather than C are considered to be interfering chains.

Our intention is to determine whether it is possible for J to miss deadline with its callback instances delayed by workload from interfering chains. From this perspective, we define the time interval [r, min{s |C| , r+D}) as the problem window of J, and focus on the execution of J's callback instances during its problem window. More specifically, we consider each callback instance c i of J with release time no later than r + D and analyze the length of time that it may be delayed by interfering chains. Without loss of generality, we let s i = r + D if s i > r +D and r i = r +D if r i > r+D. Moreover, we assume that all chain instances with deadlines earlier than J's deadline are schedulable (this assumption will be removed later in Section V). In the following, we first develop techniques which boil down the problem of bounding R(J) to bounding a value Q k related to each interfering chain C k , where Q k is a term that we develop to characterize the impact of the execution of C k to the finishing time of J. Then we bound Q k of each C k . Finally, we combine the above results and develop algorithms to perform schedulability and response time analysis.

div.head: A. Preparation
div.p: Under traditional priority-driven scheduler, e.g., fixed priority preemptive scheduling, a task can only be delayed by others with higher priority. However, this is not the case in ROS 2. Since callback instances are scheduled in batches and each callback instance executes non-preemptively, any interfering chain may have a possibility to interfere the execution of callback instances in J. In the following, we first identify the workload from interfering chains that may delay the execution of callback instances in J.

Since all chain instances with deadlines earlier than r + D are assumed to be schedulable, clearly, at most one callback instance of the same interfering chain is executing at any time in [r, r +D). Therefore, all callback instances of an interfering chain C k must execute sequentially during [r i , s i ).

div.head: V. THE SECOND BOUND
div.p: The main idea is to search all possible combinations of subinterfering sequences with regard to each individual callback instance in J, and find the one that results in maximum Q k . In other words, for each interfering chain C k , we try to identify a collection of callback instances of C k to form the interfering sequence, so that Q k is maximized. This is realized by the following steps. First, we identify the execution sequence of callback instances that may interfere with J's execution. Then we develop techniques to identify callback instances in the sequence that may contribute to Φ k,i with regard to each individual callback instance c i in J, according to whether c i can be blocked or not. Next, we present constraints to limit the searching space, and finally obtain an upper bound of Q k .

div.head: B. Callbacks that cannot be blocked
div.p: In the following, we consider the sub-interfering sequence to a callback instance c i belonging to a reentrant callback group or ∀C k ∈ Γ \ {C}: G(c i ) / ∈ θ k , i.e., c i cannot be blocked. In general, the constraints are derived based on two points. First, since the multi-threaded executor schedules callbacks from different chains in batches, c i can only be interfered by callback instances from limited number of batches. Second, once c i is added into Ω, it can only be delayed by other callback instances in Ω with higher priority than it.

It must be noticed that Ω could be updated many times when c i is blocked. Moreover, c i may also be delayed by callback instances with lower priority after c i has been added into Ω, since it could be blocked. So it is hard to bound the number of polling points during [r i , s i ) as we did in the last section. However, the following lemma can still help us to limit the possible interfering sequences.

Lemma 9 If G(c i ) ∈ ∪ ∀Ck∈Γ\{C} θ k , and more than two callbacks from C k execute during [r i , s i ), then each of them except for the first one must either belong to a different callback group from c i or have a higher priority than c i .

Proof: The lemma is proved by contradiction. Assume that more than two callback instances from C k execute during [r i , s i ), and the j th (j > 1) callback instance among them has a lower priority than c i and belongs to the same callback group as c i , which starts to execute at t, where t ∈ (r i , s i ). Then this callback must have the highest priority among all eligible callback instances in Ω at t. Moreover, since the time when it is released is later than r i , then we know c i must also have been added into Ω at t. Therefore c i must be eligible at t, reaching a contradiction with the assumption that the callback has the highest priority among all eligible callbacks at t.

Recall that we assume all chain instances with deadlines earlier than J are schedulable. Theorem 1 and 2 only hold under this assumption. In the following, we remove this assumption and derive the schedulability test for all chains. Proof: It is sufficient to prove that all chain instances with deadlines earlier than J meet their deadlines. Clearly, it is true when J is a chain instance with the earliest deadline among all chain instances. Then by Theorem 1 or 2, we know the chain instance having the earliest deadline among all chain instances except J meets its deadline. Therefore, by induction, each chain instance meets its deadline.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: In this section, we first evaluate our methods in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 by conducting experiments with both synthetic workload and case studies. Then, we compare the real-time performance of a multi-threaded executor and a single-thread executor. In particular, we show that the response time of a chain scheduled by a multi-threaded executor could be even worse than a single-threaded executor.

div.head: A. Synthetic workload
div.p: The system Γ is generated as follows: (1) The number of threads m is picked in the range [2,8]. The number of chains |Γ| is randomly picked in the range [2, n], and the number of callbacks |C i | in each chain C i is randomly picked in the range [2, b], where n and b are parameters. The period T i of C i is randomly chosen in the range [50,200], and the relative deadline D i is set to equal T i . (2) The utilization U i of each chain is generated through the UUniFast-discard algorithm [17]. The total utilization of all chains is picked in the range (0, m] which is decided by multiplying the normalized utilization U norm by m. Then we distribute the total utilization of the system to each chain. In particular, U i of each C i is no greater than 1. Through a similar way, we distribute the utilization of each chain to its individual callbacks, and the WCET of each callback is derived by multiplying its utilization by the period T i (rounded to the nearest integer). ( 3 , where a smaller number implies a higher priority. For each configuration (corresponding to one point on the x-axis of each figure), we generate 500 task systems. We compare performance of the following methods:

• OUR-1: The schedulability test performed by Theorem 3 with Theorem 1. • OUR-2: The schedulability test performed by Theorem 3 with Theorem 2. • SIMU: The maximal observed response time of each chain in simulation, assuming all chains release the first instances simultaneously, each chain releases instances as soon as possible and each callback instance executes to WCET. The simulation lasts for 5000 time units. Note that the result of SIMU is based on the measured lower bound on the actual worst-case response time. The performance is evaluated in terms of acceptance ratios, i.e., the ratio between the number of task systems that are schedulable and the number of the whole task systems (i.e., From the above results, we see that OUR-2 consistently outperforms OUR-1 under different parameter settings with a relative large gap. In particular, we can observe that the result of OUR-2 is lower than SIMU, indicating that our method is safe. However, there is still a margin between SIMU and OUR-2. One reason is that SIMU is a lower bound instead of a safe bound, which is measured within a relative short time interval (the simulation is very time consuming, and we are not able to run simulations for a long time while keeping reasonable sample size). Nevertheless, we think there is still large room to improve the test. A straightforward improvement is to consider all combinations of "carry in"and "carry out" callback instances to obtain more precise -→ M k of each interfering chain C k (which in the paper is assumed to comprise the whole chain instances of maximum number), and thus obtain a tighter response time bound (due to the space limitation, we do not present the algorithm here but the intuition). We can also develop more constraints to derive more precise tests, which can be easily extended with our method. We will consider these improvements in our future work.

div.head: B. Case studies
div.p: In the next, we evaluate our analysis techniques with case studies. We also present empirical evaluation to demonstrate the performance difference under single-thread executor and multi-threaded executor. The case studies are deployed in ROS 2 Foxy Fitzroy, running on top of Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS with kernel 5.4.0-113-generic and a PC with Intel i5-7500 CPU (two cores are used to serve a multi-threaded executor). A brief description of the case studies is shown in TABLE V. We run each for 5 minutes on a multi-threaded executor with 2 threads and a single-threaded executor, respectively, and measure the average-case response time (ACRT) and worstcase response time (WCRT) of each chain (which is a lower bound instead of a safe one).

The first case study is quoted from sub-chains in Fig. 10 developed by Choi et al. in [13] from realistic autonomous driving systems. All callbacks are considered to be in reentrant callback groups. We compute the response time bound of each chain by Theorem 2 (the system is schedulable according to An interesting problem we observed is that the response time of a chain scheduled by a multi-threaded executor could be much worse than the single-threaded executor. In particular, even all callbacks are in the same mutually exclusive group, the scheduling under multi-threaded executor where all callbacks are forced to execute sequentially is much different from that under the single-threaded executor. We use the second case study to show the problem. All callbacks are assigned to the same mutually exclusive group. The results are shown in TABLE VI. We can see that the response time of the third chain under the multi-threaded scheduler is much larger than that under the single-threaded executor. This is because, under a multi-threaded executor, a callback instance can be blocked and removed from wait set, which may be added in wait set later together with newly ready callback instances with higher priority than it. At this time, a callback instance with higher priority will be scheduled first. As a result, this callback instance is blocked again and then removed from wait set. This situation may repeat several times to make this callback instance blocked by other higher priority callback instances over and over. In contrast, under a single-threaded executor, a callback instance will not be removed from wait set, and thus cannot be blocked by callback instances that are not added in wait set at the same time with it. A part of the resulting sequences of the second case study is shown in Fig. 7, which is generated with the tracing tool ROS2 tracing [11]. A chain instance of each chain is released simultaneously at the time marked by red arrow. We can see that the instance of c 3,1 is delayed by two instances from each of C 1 and C 2 under the multi-threaded executor. However, the instance of c 3,1 is only delayed by one instance from each of C 1 and C 2 under the single-threaded executor. This result suggests that, we must carefully consider the assignment of callback groups for callbacks when implementing a system on multi-threaded executor or merging callbacks from multiple single-threaded executors into a multi-threaded one.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: There has been plentiful work targeting on improving realtime performance in ROS [18], [19], [22]. For example, [23] proposed a real-time extension on transparent CPU/GPU coordination mechanism. [14] studied the end-to-end latency of ROS 2 for distributed systems. [9] replaced the standard rclcpp Executor in ROS 2 with a real-time executor called the Callback-group-level Executor, and explored the resulting performance. However, these studies only improve the real-time capability but not provide any analytical real-time guarantee.

Casini et.al conducted the first work [8] on formal modeling and analysis of ROS 2 executor, and modeled the scheduling behaviors of single-threaded executors, laying foundation for subsequent analysis. [10] improved the response time analysis techniques and proposed priority assignment strategies to optimize response time. [12] improved [8] by considering the variance of actual execution time and further exploring scheduling features in ROS 2. [13] proposed a new priority-driven chainaware scheduler for the ROS 2 framework and conduct endto-end latency analysis for the proposed scheduler. [24] introduced the ROS Live latency manager (ROSLlama), which used existing real-time mechanisms to control end-to-end latency and automatically estimated all required scheduling parameters at run-time. Specially, [24] relies on the results in [8] to bound the response time. In summary, all existing work focuses on the analysis of single-threaded executors.

Despite works on ROS 2, analysis of processing chains has also been studied. There are mainly two categories: data chain [25], [26], where tasks in the chain are triggered individually, and trigger chain, where tasks are triggered by their predecessors. In the wide sense, the processing chain on ROS 2 executors considered in this paper belongs to the trigger chain category. Two of the most popular frameworks for analyzing response time of trigger chains are Compositional Performance Analysis [27] and Real-Time Calculus [28], based on which [29] calculated the response time for a sequence of threads with synchronous and asynchronous communication, [30] optimized the end-to-end latency of a trigger chain traversing multiple processors. For traditional non-preemptive scheduling of sequential real-time tasks on multiprocessors, [31] proposed a sufficient but not necessary polynomial-time schedulability test condition for periodic tasks scheduled under EDF. [32] proposed new sufficient tests with linear-time complexity under EDF, and further presented improved test conditions of pseudo-polynomial time complexity for EDF and FP scheduling, respectively. Nevertheless, all these work cannot capture the specific scheduling features of ROS 2 executors, and thus can not be directly applied.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this work, we present the scheduling model of systems implemented as processing chains that are deployed on a multi-threaded executor, and develop response time analysis techniques for them. We also identify a risk of increasing response time when merging workload from multiple singlethreaded executors into one multi-threaded executor. In our future work, we will extend our techniques to more general and complex settings, such as chains with arbitrary deadlines, as well as systems in directed cyclic graph model where chains may have some common callbacks.
